extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of philosophy; readers of Montaigne/early-modern essays
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and interpretation of Montaigne's essay on the soul and human knowledge; assessing his argumentative stance and rhetorical examples. Useful for students of philosophy or literature studying skepticism about human reason and early‑modern thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human reason is fallible
rubrics_metrics.description: Human reason and philosophical inquiry produce many gross mistakes, silly arguments, and contradictory opinions—even among the greatest thinkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne adduces many examples (Plato’s defining man as a two‑legged featherless animal, Epicurean atoms needing hooked tails, contradictory locations of the soul by Hippocrates, Aristotle, Stoics, Epicurus, etc.) to show that celebrated philosophers nonetheless make absurd or imprudent claims; he draws the lesson that we should judge human wisdom modestly and with distrust of its pretensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not demand metaphysical exactness about the soul’s figure or habitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about the precise figure of the soul or the part of the body it inhabits are not to be inquired into.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted formula: “Quâ facie quidem sit animus, aut ubi habitet, ne quorendum quidem est.” Montaigne relays Cicero’s sentiment and prefers to leave such metaphysical minutiae aside rather than force exact anatomical assignments for the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground claims about the soul in observable present effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The relevant powers and effects of the soul should be assessed by its present condition and observable operations in life, especially insofar as bodily injuries immediately affect its faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues for locating the soul’s practical consideration in the present (e.g., wounds to the brain immediately offend faculties), and uses empirical examples—disease, intoxication, madness, effects of a mad dog’s bite, preservation/decline with age—to support judgments about the soul’s relation to the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer humility/faith where human reason is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: For questions such as the soul’s immortality, Montaigne counsels reliance on divine revelation and humility rather than overconfident human proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He argues that the immortality of the soul is a belief better received from God and faith than derived from human reason, since human arguments are weak and contested: “It was truly very good reason that we should be beholden to God only… and faith; for ‘tis no lesson of nature and our own reason.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of rhetorical disguises and public accommodations of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers sometimes conceal or alter their real opinions to accommodate public reception, using poetry, fable, or other disguises; one should be aware of this rhetorical practice when evaluating their claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes that thinkers often ‘disguise’ or falsify their real opinions for public use and that crude philosophical matter is sometimes dressed to suit audiences; this counsels interpretive caution and sensitivity to rhetorical masking of true beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test speculative doctrines by practical consequences and internal coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculative systems (e.g., transmigration of souls, atomic theories) should be tested for internal plausibility and practical consequences; absurd implications undermine credence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne highlights opponents’ objections (Epicureans’ objection to transmigration when births/deaths mismatch; absurd consequences of atoms falling in parallel lines unless ad hoc motions are appended) to show that theories that imply absurd situations or require ad hoc devices are suspect. He uses reductio and concrete thought‑experiments to evaluate doctrines.
